solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Escorted by an idiot, as duke and duchess are?

parts.note: a tit is British slang for a fool
to escort someone is to lead them

explanation.surface: An aristocratic couple being shown around by a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Escorted by an idiot' reads as a picture of the couple, but it is an instruction: the escort word follows the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Dukes and duchesses hold hereditary noble ranks, so each of them carries a formal rank of nobility.

clue.text: Foot of Everest? I'm sure yeti lives here?

indicators.note: the foot of a word written down is its bottom, so its closing letter is wanted

parts.note: the mountain's final letter
'I bet' is a way of saying you are certain

explanation.surface: A musing on whether the abominable snowman makes its home at the base of the world's highest mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot of Everest' looks like a place but gives only a letter; the question mark flags that the yeti's home is legend, not fact.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan region north of Everest is the traditional homeland of the legendary yeti, the abominable snowman.

clue.text: Advice on fluffy dog from Spooner? I'm off!

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his version of a phrase has its initial sounds exchanged

parts.note: a tip about a poodle, the curly-coated breed; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: Someone asked for grooming advice about their fluffy pet announces a hasty exit instead.
explanation.walkthrough: A poodle tip is advice on a fluffy dog; exchanging the P and T sounds gives the old-fashioned British farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a jaunty, dated British way of saying goodbye, the parting words of someone leaving.

clue.text: Some upset chihuahUAS Exasperate a hairy man

indicators.note: to upset is to overturn, and in a down clue an overturned run of letters reads from bottom to top
'some' asks for only part of the following text, a run of letters sitting inside it

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of the dog's name and the start of the verb

explanation.surface: Bad-tempered little dogs driving a shaggy fellow up the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis calls Jacob's twin a hairy man, which is the standard crossword route to this name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Jacob's elder twin brother is described as a hairy man, contrasted with smooth-skinned Jacob.

clue.text: Wallops Liberal moving to the right? Rubbish!

indicators.note: a letter shifting along the word is taken out of its place and set back in further along

parts.note: to wallop someone is to hit them hard
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A political outburst dismissing a Liberal's shift rightwards as a load of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The L moves from second place in the word for beats to fifth. 'Moving to the right' reads as a political drift but is literal: along the line of letters. Cobblers is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobblers is British rhyming slang (cobbler's awls) used as an exclamation meaning nonsense or talk not worth hearing.

clue.text: Strange time to admit army scrap

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece takes another inside it

parts.note: odd means strange
an army is made of men
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An odd moment for the army to own up to a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a fight to go with army; it is a leftover bit.
explanation.definitionFit: A leftover remnant or odd piece of material is a scrap, the bit remaining when the rest is used.

clue.text: Matron's rib broken? This might solve the problem

indicators.note: something broken falls to pieces, so these letters are scattered and put back in a new order

parts.note: the letters used as written

explanation.surface: A hospital matron has a fractured rib and a remedy is proposed.
explanation.walkthrough: The matron's broken rib suggests a medical problem, but the fix is a session of group thinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A group session of pooling ideas quickly is a common method for finding a way out of a difficulty.

clue.text: Revolutionary sailor inspired by old English muse

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the letters are turned to read the other way
to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece is drawn inside another

parts.note: OE is the abbreviation for Old English
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A rebellious seaman takes his inspiration from an old English poetic muse.
explanation.walkthrough: The sailor goes inside OE, and the whole is then turned round. 'Revolutionary' looks like a description of the sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she is one of the nine Muses, presiding over lyric and love poetry.

clue.text: Become very worried about sons getting into beer

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so these letters go inside another word

parts.note: stout is a dark beer
re means about or concerning
S is the abbreviation for son, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A parent frets over their sons taking to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is not a link here: it gives RE, which joins the doubled S inside the dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to get into a state of anxiety and tension, the same as growing very anxious.

clue.text: Staff did a runner, I hear, leading to complaint

parts.note: to staff a post is to man it

indicators.note: what one hears is the sound, not the spelling, so a word spelt differently but said the same is wanted

parts.note: someone who fled flew the coop

explanation.surface: An employee fled the premises, which led to a grievance being lodged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' looks like a grievance; it is an ailment. Man flu is a jokey British term for a mild cold that a man treats as serious illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can be a minor illness, and this is a mild cold exaggerated by the male sufferer.

clue.text: Bishop I love getting a bit reactionary? Details here

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
taken as written
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

indicators.note: a reactionary wants to go backwards, so these letters are read back to front

parts.note: a tad is a small amount

explanation.surface: A bishop confesses to loving being a little conservative in his views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reactionary' looks like a political description of the bishop, but it only turns the small amount round.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a summary of a person's life and career, a document where personal particulars are set out.

clue.text: Silence on radio as very bright female chucked out

parts.note: dead means very, as in dead easy

indicators.note: something chucked out is thrown away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: fair weather is bright
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A radio station goes quiet because a brilliant female presenter has been sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' is the colloquial intensifier, as in 'dead right'; the female's letter is thrown out of the bright weather word.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasters use this term for an unintended gap in transmission when nothing is heard by listeners.

clue.text: Charge for ring

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fee paid to use a road or bridge
second meaning: to sound a bell slowly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge for ring' suggests a phone fee; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a payment demanded for passage along a road and the slow ringing of a bell.

clue.text: A sonnet for turbulent times

indicators.note: turbulent means stirred up and disordered, so these letters are tossed into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters used as written
the letters used as written, part of the mix

explanation.surface: A poem written for troubled days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word but its letters belong in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The periods of each day after noon are particular parts of the day, so they are times.

clue.text: Does this tell you what's wrong with Conservative nieces misbehaving?

definitions.text: Does this tell you what's wrong

parts.note: con is the Italian for with, as in con brio

indicators.note: to misbehave is to act out of order, so these letters are put out of order

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
the letters used as written

explanation.surface: A Tory politician's nieces are behaving badly, and something should be pricking someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word but is Italian, as in musical directions like con brio; the Conservative's letter joins the nieces in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The inner moral sense is the faculty that warns a person when an action is morally bad.

clue.text: Chance result of Times expert going by Tube

parts.note: three times four is three by four
a pro is an expert
a duct is a tube

explanation.surface: A Times crossword expert takes the London Underground and something happens by chance.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals on Times and Tube point to the newspaper and the London Underground; both are plain words. 'By' as multiplication is used in measurements like six by four.
explanation.definitionFit: A secondary thing produced incidentally, not the main aim, is an unplanned outcome of a process.

clue.text: Last drink? Your very good health!

parts.note: the one at the bottom of a list is last
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Raising one final glass before closing time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last drink?' reads as a call for one more round; the words are split into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are drinking toasts said while raising glasses, wishing companions well before everyone drains their drinks.

clue.text: Beat policemen heading back by river

indicators.note: heading back is going the opposite way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police
the Po is the main river of northern Italy

explanation.surface: Police officers on their beat walk back along the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' suggests the police patrol route, but it is the musical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the speed of the underlying pulse is the rate at which a piece is played.

clue.text: The sauce of these two girls!

definitions.text: The sauce of these two girls!

parts.words: The sauce of these two girls!
parts.note: surface reading: an exclamation at the cheek of a pair of young women

parts.words: The sauce of these two girls!
parts.note: setter's reading: a condiment whose name is two girls' first names put together

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at the impudence of two cheeky girls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' in the surface means cheek; the answer is the pink sauce served with a British prawn cocktail, named with two girls' names.
explanation.definitionFit: The pink mayonnaise-and-ketchup dressing for prawn cocktail bears two female first names side by side.

clue.text: Sat around, having eaten old man's grub

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards
what is eaten ends up inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

explanation.surface: Someone lounged about after polishing off their father's food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sat around' reads as lazing about; it is the word turned round. Old man is slang for father.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub is slang for food, and these are Spanish small savoury dishes served as snacks.

clue.text: Soldier's daughter retreats in confusion

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter

indicators.note: things in confusion are jumbled up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters used as written

explanation.surface: A soldier's daughter falls back in disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldier's' looks possessive, but the 's is just 'is' linking definition to wordplay. The Desert Rats were the British 7th Armoured Division in the WWII North Africa campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of Britain's 7th Armoured Division, famed in North African desert fighting, was a serviceman of that unit.

clue.text: Money companion's invested in play

indicators.note: money invested is put into something, so one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: a play is a drama
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A friend's cash has been put into a theatre production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' suits money, drawing the eye to finance, but it only puts one piece inside another. Companion of Honour is a British honour abbreviated CH.
explanation.definitionFit: It was the currency unit of Greece before the euro, so it is a form of cash.

clue.text: Very fast stretch of water

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: A description of a swift-flowing channel of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed but means going without food, the season before Easter. The Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and mainland England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the named strait separating the Isle of Wight from Hampshire on the English south coast.

clue.text: Novel extremely lively to begin with

parts.note: novel means new and original

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its first and last letters count

parts.note: the two end letters of the word

explanation.surface: A book that is very lively in its opening pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book but is the adjective meaning new.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means at first or initially, describing how things stood at the start.

clue.text: Silly way Emma begins

wordplay.note: the name opens with the fifth letter of the alphabet, so the way it starts is with that letter preceded by a preposition and an article

explanation.surface: A foolish manner in which a heroine starts her story.
explanation.walkthrough: The way Emma begins is 'in an E': she starts with that letter. 'Way' looks like a path or road but means manner.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means foolish, empty-headed and lacking sense, just like something daft or pointless.

clue.text: Auntie to take two books about Europe on vacation

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the outer pair goes round the middle

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book, taken twice

indicators.note: a place on vacation is left empty, so only the outside letters of the word remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of the continent's name

explanation.surface: An aunt packs a couple of books to read on a European holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie and the Beeb are both British nicknames for the BBC. 'Vacation' is holiday, but here it means emptying the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are affectionate British nicknames for the BBC, the national public broadcaster.

clue.text: Become British, getting picture from police?

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
an E-fit is a computer-made likeness of a suspect built from witness descriptions

explanation.surface: Someone takes British citizenship and ends up with their image on a police poster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Become British' reads as naturalising; 'Become' alone is the definition, in the sense of suiting.
explanation.definitionFit: When a hat becomes you it suits you; to be suitable or appropriate for someone is the same sense.

clue.text: A singer engaged in dubious activity?

parts.note: taken as written
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A vocalist mixed up in something shady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' suggests a performer; it is a bird. The phrase is British slang for being up to no good.
explanation.definitionFit: In British idiom someone who is up to mischief or misbehaving is said to be doing something shady.

clue.text: It's true, Seth occasionally has a funny feeling up north

indicators.note: in northern English speech the opening aitch is dropped, so that first letter goes
occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is used

parts.note: the first and third letters of the name
taken as written
a hunch is an odd intuitive feeling

explanation.surface: Seth admits that he sometimes gets a strange sensation when in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern English accents famously drop the H, so a hunch said up north loses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A loyal and steadfast supporter is one who remains faithful, the sense of true as in true to a cause.

clue.text: Put heads together to make this dish

indicators.note: putting things together sets them side by side, so the pieces are joined in a row
together means joined up, so the pieces run on one after the other

parts.note: one slang word for the head
another slang word for the head, as in 'use your loaf'

explanation.surface: People confer to plan a recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put heads together' means confer, but here it joins two slang terms for the head, nut and loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a vegetarian baked dish made from chopped nuts and breadcrumbs, shaped in a tin and sliced.

clue.text: Common to see biplane flying round east?

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one piece goes outside another
things flying are tossed about in the air, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters used as written
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A double-winged aircraft circling eastward is a commonplace sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common' looks like 'often seen', but it means lowly or of the ordinary people.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the ordinary people rather than the upper classes, and so lowly or vulgar in origin.

clue.text: Confirm where international cricket fan might be?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to bear witness that something is true

definitions.text: where international cricket fan might be?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: present at a Test, a full international cricket match

explanation.walkthrough: A Test is a full international cricket match, so a fan watching one is at it; the question mark flags the split reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare or bear witness that something is so is to verify it, making it certain.
